## Story

> Night shift at the customs office on Pier 9, Port of Kleeberg. At 04:30 the MV Kestrel comes alongside with 40 containers, and at 07:00 she sails again.
>
> The XR-90 scanner, which used to pick them, crashed at midnight and won't boot. What the office still has: the log of 3,000 inspections from the last two years, each with its measurements and what was found inside, and the notes of the people who did this job before.
>
> Teach a model to tell the smugglers from the rest. This room loads Python with pandas and scikit-learn, so the first puzzle you open takes a little while.

## Stations

### 1. The inspector's rule card

**Practises:** Decision trees: features and target, max_depth, reading thresholds with export_text, why the target must not be a feature  
**Needs:** 🔎 Hanne's rule card  
**Data:** [inspections.py](../../content/rooms/ml-customs/data/inspections.py)

**Task:**

> Hanne Lindqvist inspected containers on Pier 9 for thirty years and decided by a rule card she drew herself: three questions, one after another. The card is still pinned above her old desk, but someone rubbed out the numbers.
>
> The last two years of inspections are loaded as `inspections`, one row per opened container: how much heavier it was than declared (`weight_gap_pct`), the declared value per kg in euros, days in transit, the route's risk class (1 to 5), the X-ray image's density, the old scanner's alarm (`old_flag`) and what was inside (`contraband`, 1 = contraband).
>
> 1. Grow a decision tree that is three questions deep on the measurements, to predict `contraband`.
> 2. Print it with `export_text` and compare it with Hanne's card.
> 3. Enter the number rubbed out of the **first** question: the weight gap, in percent.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

# inspections is loaded: 3,000 past inspections, indexed by inspection number.
print(inspections.head())

X = inspections                  # what the tree may look at
y = inspections["contraband"]    # what it should predict

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns)))
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])
y = inspections["contraband"]
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns)))
```

**Answer:** `8.5`

**Reveals when solved:**

> Hanne's first question is back: **is the container more than 8.5 % heavier than declared?** Both answers lead to a question about the X-ray density (above 1.21 on the light side, above 0.94 on the heavy side), and only then to a verdict.
>
> A decision tree is exactly such a card: questions about one feature at a time, each with a threshold the tree picked from the data. The starter's tree asked one question only, about `contraband` itself: a tree that may look at the answer learns nothing else.

**Hints:**

1. Run the starter. The tree asks a single question, and it is about `contraband`. What does `X` contain?
2. `X` must hold only what an inspector knows before opening the container. Hanne's card also says she never looked at the scanner's alarm. `inspections.drop(columns=[...])` removes columns.
3. `X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])`. The first line of `export_text` is the first question: `weight_gap_pct <= ...`.

### 2. The proud dashboard

**Practises:** The accuracy paradox with a rare class: confusion matrix, precision and recall, classification_report  
**Needs:** 🔎 The XR-90 poster  
**Data:** [inspections.py](../../content/rooms/ml-customs/data/inspections.py)

**Task:**

> The screen above the night desk still shows the XR-90's record. The scanner looked at every container of the last two years, and `old_flag` in `inspections` says where it raised the alarm (1) and where it stayed quiet (0). How good was it at catching smugglers?
>
> 1. Compare `old_flag` with `contraband`: the confusion matrix and the classification report.
> 2. Store `accuracy` (the share of containers the scanner judged right), `missed` (contraband containers it let through) and `recall` (the share of contraband it flagged).
> 3. Your verdict: would you trust the XR-90 to pick the containers? Store `trust` (`True` or `False`).

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report

y = inspections["contraband"]    # 1 = contraband found when opened
flag = inspections["old_flag"]   # 1 = the XR-90 raised its alarm

accuracy = None  # share of containers the scanner judged right
missed = None    # contraband containers the scanner let through
recall = None    # share of the contraband it flagged
trust = None     # True or False
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report, accuracy_score, recall_score

y = inspections["contraband"]
flag = inspections["old_flag"]
print(confusion_matrix(y, flag))
print(classification_report(y, flag))

accuracy = accuracy_score(y, flag)
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y, flag).ravel()
missed = int(fn)
recall = recall_score(y, flag)
trust = bool(recall > 0.5)
print(accuracy, missed, recall, trust)
```

**Checked result** (`_dashboard_check(accuracy, missed, recall, trust)`):

```json
"exposed"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> 93.5 % right, and almost useless. Of 207 contraband containers the XR-90 flagged **25** and let **182** through: a recall of 12 %. It was right so often because 93 % of all containers are clean, and it called nearly everything clean.
>
> When one class is rare, accuracy says little. Ask what the confusion matrix asks: how many of the cases you care about did the model catch (recall), and how many of its alarms were real (precision)?

**Hints:**

1. The poster beside the screen makes a claim about the XR-90; put it to the test. `print(confusion_matrix(y, flag))`: rows are what was really inside (0, 1), columns what the scanner said (0, 1).
2. The scanner missed a container when it was contraband (row 1) and the scanner said clean (column 0). `tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y, flag).ravel()` unpacks the four cells.
3. `missed = fn` and `recall = tp / (tp + fn)`, or `recall_score(y, flag)` from `sklearn.metrics`. `print(classification_report(y, flag))` shows precision and recall for both classes. `accuracy_score(y, flag)` is 93.5 %, but a recall of 12 % means `trust = False`.

### 3. The neighbours

**Practises:** k-nearest neighbours: scaling in a Pipeline, GridSearchCV over n_neighbors with cross-validation, choosing a metric (F1) for a rare class  
**Needs:** 🔎 Jonas's note on the terminal, 🔎 The harbour master's audit rule  
**Data:** [inspections.py](../../content/rooms/ml-customs/data/inspections.py)

**Task:**

> Jonas from the day shift had an idea before he went home: judge each new container by the past inspections that look most like it, its nearest neighbours. His terminal still shows the attempt. How many neighbours judge a container best?
>
> 1. Split the inspections into a training and a test part.
> 2. Search for the best number of neighbours with `GridSearchCV` on the training part. Store the fitted search as `search`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from helpers import show_plot

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])   # the five measurements
y = inspections["contraband"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y)   # the training and test part

model = KNeighborsClassifier()
search = GridSearchCV(model, {"n_neighbors": [5]}, scoring="accuracy", cv=5)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(search.best_params_, round(search.best_score_, 3))

# Who are the five nearest neighbours of the first training container?
dist, idx = model.fit(X_train, y_train).kneighbors(X_train.iloc[:1])
print(X_train.iloc[idx[0]])
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from helpers import show_plot

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])
y = inspections["contraband"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=9)

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier())
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 32, 2))}, scoring="f1", cv=5)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(search.best_params_, round(search.best_score_, 3))
show_plot(pd.Series(search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"], index=range(1, 32, 2)), title="F1 by k")
```

**Checked result** (`_neighbours_check(search)`):

```json
"neighbourly"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> **k = 5.** With every feature scaled, five neighbours give the best F1 on the training folds (about 0.62); fewer copy the noise of single inspections, more drown the rare smugglers in clean neighbours.
>
> Without scaling, the neighbours were simply the containers with the most similar price per kg: a difference of 100 € outweighed any weight gap or X-ray image, and the best F1 was about 0.34. KNN measures distances, so it needs the scaler, and inside a pipeline the scaler is fitted on each training fold only.

**Hints:**

1. Use the split from the harbour master's rule: `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=9)`. Jonas's note on the screen says how he wanted to search. Then look at the neighbours the starter prints: which column do they agree on?
2. `value_per_kg` runs into the thousands, so it decides every distance. `make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier())` scales first. In a pipeline the grid's key gets the step's name: `kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors`.
3. `search = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 32, 2))}, scoring="f1", cv=5)`, then `search.fit(X_train, y_train)` and `search.best_params_`.

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from helpers import show_plot

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])
y = inspections["contraband"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=9)

train_scores = []
test_scores = []
for depth in range(1, 16):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    train_scores.append(tree.score(X_train, y_train))
    test_scores.append(tree.score(X_test, y_test))

depths = range(1, 16)
show_plot(pd.Series(train_scores, index=depths), pd.Series(test_scores, index=depths), labels=["train", "test"], title="Accuracy by depth")
print(pd.Series(test_scores, index=depths).round(4))
depth = 3
```

**Checked result** (`_depth_check(train_scores, test_scores, depth)`):

```json
"pruned"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> **Depth 3.** The training score climbs with every level, to 99.6 % at depth 15, but the test score peaks at depth 3 (96.5 %) and then falls: the deeper tree learns the quirks of single training containers, which no new container shares. That is overfitting, and Hanne's card was exactly as deep as it should be.
>
> A score on the training data says how well a model remembers; only the test part says how well it judges.

**Hints:**

1. The harbour master's rule gives every argument of the split: `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=9)`.
2. In the loop: `tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)`, then append `tree.score(X_train, y_train)` and `tree.score(X_test, y_test)`.
3. The training curve always rises, so it can't choose. The best depth is where the test curve is highest: `pd.Series(test_scores, index=range(1, 16)).idxmax()`.

### 5. The odds board

**Practises:** Logistic regression: coefficients on standardised features, predict_proba, moving the decision threshold to trade precision for recall  
**Needs:** 🔒 2. The proud dashboard, 🔎 The chief's order, 🔎 The harbour master's audit rule  
**Data:** [inspections.py](../../content/rooms/ml-customs/data/inspections.py)

**Code lock** (opens with `182`):

> The board's control panel is under a cover with a three-digit padlock. Scratched into the frame: "Combination = how many smugglers the XR-90 let through in two years."

**Task:**

> The big board on the wall shows each container's chance of contraband, from a logistic regression, and a dial sets from which chance on a container gets opened. At 0.5 the board opens few containers, and lets many smugglers through. Where should the dial stand?
>
> 1. Fit `LogisticRegression` on the standardised training part, as `model`.
> 2. Its coefficients say how much each feature raises the odds. Store the column name of the riskiest feature as `riskiest`.
> 3. Set the dial: store its step as `threshold`, and how many containers of the test part it opens as `opened`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])   # the five measurements
y = inspections["contraband"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y)   # the training and test part

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model[-1].coef_)   # one coefficient per column of X, in order
riskiest = None          # the column name with the largest coefficient

p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]   # each test container's chance of contraband
print((p >= 0.5).sum(), "opened, recall", recall_score(y_test, p >= 0.5))

threshold = None   # the dial's step
opened = None      # test containers opened at that step
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])
y = inspections["contraband"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=9)

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X_train, y_train)
coefs = pd.Series(model[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns).sort_values()
print(coefs.round(2))
riskiest = coefs.idxmax()

p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
for t in [0.5, 0.45, 0.4, 0.35, 0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05]:
    print(t, round(recall_score(y_test, p >= t), 3), (p >= t).sum())
threshold = 0.15
opened = int((p >= threshold).sum())
```

**Checked result** (`_odds_check(model, riskiest, threshold, opened)`):

```json
"calibrated"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The weight gap weighs most (coefficient 1.49 per standard deviation), then the X-ray density (1.21); the price per kg barely matters. At 0.5 the board caught only half the smugglers. Turned down to **0.15**, it catches 83 % of them and opens **76** of the 750 test containers.
>
> A classifier gives probabilities; the threshold is a decision you make, by weighing missed smugglers against opened boxes. Lowering it buys recall with precision.

**Hints:**

1. Split as the harbour master's rule says, and set the dial as the chief's order on the wall says. `model[-1]` is the pipeline's last step, the logistic regression; `pd.Series(model[-1].coef_[0], index=X.columns)` names each coefficient.
2. `p >= t` opens every container with a chance of at least `t`. For each step on the dial (0.5, 0.45, … 0.05), print `recall_score(y_test, p >= t)` and `(p >= t).sum()`.
3. Go down the dial and stop at the first step whose recall is at least 0.8: that is `threshold`. `opened = int((p >= threshold).sum())`.

**Code lock** (opens with `3576`):

> The crane console is locked with a four-digit PIN. The chief's note next to it: "PIN = the overgrown tree's best depth, then the neighbours' best k, then how many test containers the odds board opens."

**Task:**

> The MV Kestrel is alongside. Its manifest lists tonight's 40 containers, loaded as `arrivals` and indexed by container number, with the same measurements as the inspections: the scanner's alarm is missing, since the scanner is down. The crane can set down four containers before the ship sails: which four?
>
> 1. Train the model you trust most on the inspections, as `model`.
> 2. Score all 40 arrivals with `predict_proba`.
> 3. Store the container numbers of the four riskiest as `opened`.

<details><summary>Starter code</summary>

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

print(arrivals.head())   # tonight's 40 containers, indexed by container number

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])   # the five measurements
y = inspections["contraband"]
model = None   # your best model, trained on the inspections

risk = None    # each arrival's chance of contraband
opened = []    # the four container numbers to open
```

</details>

**Model solution:**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X = inspections.drop(columns=["old_flag", "contraband"])
y = inspections["contraband"]
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X, y)

risk = pd.Series(model.predict_proba(arrivals[X.columns])[:, 1], index=arrivals.index)
risk = risk.sort_values(ascending=False)
print(risk.head(8).round(3))
opened = risk.index[:4].tolist()
```

**Checked result** (`_arrivals_check(model, opened)`):

```json
"opened"
```

**Reveals when solved:**

> The crane sets down containers 4365, 4537, 4643 and 4761, and in each one the crew finds a false wall full of cigarettes. Every model you could trust put the same four on top: heavy beyond their papers, dense on the X-ray, on risky routes. The decoys stayed on the ship: the dense crate of machine parts the old scanner would have opened, the risky route with honest cargo, the heavy load of tiles that was simply declared wrong.
>
> The Kestrel sails at seven. The XR-90 gets a new job: holding the door of the night office open.

**Hints:**

1. The crane schedule says what test the chief puts every model through. Any of tonight's models will do if it is trained well: a tree of the depth that won at the filing cabinet, a scaled KNN with the neighbours' k, or the odds board's logistic regression. Train it on `X` and `y` (all inspections, without `old_flag`).
2. `model.predict_proba(arrivals)` fails: the manifest lists the columns in another order. `arrivals[X.columns]` puts them in the order the model learned.
3. `risk = pd.Series(model.predict_proba(arrivals[X.columns])[:, 1], index=arrivals.index).sort_values(ascending=False)`, then `opened = risk.index[:4].tolist()`.

## Clues in the room

### 🔎 Hanne's rule card

*Used by: 1. The inspector's rule card*

> A postcard-sized card, drawn in pencil, the numbers rubbed out:
>
> **1.** Heavier than declared by more than ▒▒ %?
> · no → **2a.** X-ray density above ▒▒? Then one more question about the weight.
> · yes → **2b.** X-ray density above ▒▒? Then one more question.
>
> Written along the edge: "Three questions, never more. I never trusted the scanner's beeping, and you only know what's inside once it's open."

### 🔎 The XR-90 poster

*Used by: 2. The proud dashboard*

> A glossy poster from the manufacturer:
>
> **XR-90 · 93.5 % right!**
> Two years on Pier 9 and hardly a false alarm.

### 🔎 The harbour master's audit rule

*Used by: 3. The neighbours, 4. The overgrown tree, 5. The odds board*

> PORT OF KLEEBERG · audit rule 7
>
> A model is judged on containers it has never seen. Hold back a quarter of the inspections as the test part (**test_size=0.25**), with the same share of contraband in both parts (**stratify=y**), and use **random_state=9** (Pier 9), so that every shift gets the same split.

### 🔎 Jonas's note on the terminal

*Used by: 3. The neighbours*

> "KNN for the night shift, my plan:
>
> · try every **odd** k from **1 to 31** (odd, so the neighbours can't tie)
> · not by accuracy: opening nothing already gets 93 %. By **F1**, which needs caught smugglers *and* few wasted openings: **scoring="f1"**
> · **5 folds** on the training part
>
> The neighbours it picks look strange to me, though: always about the same price per kg? — J."

### 🔎 The chief's order

*Used by: 5. The odds board*

> From Chief Inspector Mirković, for the night shift:
>
> The odds board's dial goes down from **0.50** in steps of **0.05**. Set it to the **highest** step that still catches at least **4 in 5** smugglers on the test part (recall ≥ 0.8). Every step lower opens more boxes, and we don't have the hands for that.

### 🔎 Tonight's crane schedule

*Used by: 6. The crane console*

> MV Kestrel · berth Pier 9 · 40 containers · alongside 04:30, sails 07:00
>
> The chief's test for any model: the academy keeps 1,000 sealed past inspections with 70 smuggling cases. Among the **100** your model scores riskiest, at least **40** of those cases must be found.

## Handbook in the room: 📖 The night shift's classification binder

**Features, target and the split:** [`X = df.drop(columns=["a", "b"])  y = df["c"]`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.drop.html), [`train_test_split(X, y, test_size=, stratify=, random_state=)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split.html), [`model.fit(X, y)  model.predict(X)  model.score(X, y)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/getting_started.html#fitting-and-predicting-estimator-basics)

**Decision trees:** [`DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=, random_state=)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier.html), [`export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X.columns))`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.tree.export_text.html), [`overfitting`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_underfitting_overfitting.html)

**Judging a classifier:** [`confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix.html), [`accuracy, precision, recall, F1`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html#precision-recall-f-measure-metrics), [`accuracy_score  precision_score  recall_score  f1_score`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.recall_score.html), [`classification_report(y_true, y_pred)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.classification_report.html)

**Nearest neighbours and searching settings:** [`KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.neighbors.KNeighborsClassifier.html), [`StandardScaler()`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html), [`make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.make_pipeline.html), [`GridSearchCV(model, param_grid, scoring=, cv=)`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV.html)

**Logistic regression and thresholds:** [`LogisticRegression()`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.html), [`model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.html#sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.predict_proba), [`p >= threshold`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/classification_threshold.html)

**New data:** [`df[X.columns]`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/indexing.html#basics), [`pd.Series(values, index=df.index).sort_values(ascending=False)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.sort_values.html)
